name: Livagen

lead: Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala) is a short peptide from Khavinson's group in Russia, described as a regulator of gene activity in ageing cells. Forum users pitch it as a non-injectable-style anti-aging option meant to keep cells acting younger and, in turn, looking younger.

The chain runs from chromatin and gene-expression effects to cells behaving younger to a younger appearance. Researchers report that it loosens condensed heterochromatin and activates ribosomal genes in lymphocytes from older donors, and stimulates liver tissue growth in culture. Studies are small and mostly in cell cultures and rats; skin, hair and bone have not been tested in people.

paras: It is used in periodic courses as part of broader longevity stacks, often with other bioregulator peptides. Users describe expecting slow, cumulative effects over months.
No human safety data was found. It is sold online as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine, so product purity and legal status vary by country.

angle.text: Livagen is pitched by forum users as a peptide that makes cells act younger, which they hope shows up as younger-looking skin, hair and tissue. Lab work reports chromatin changes in cells from older donors; visible ageing has not been tested in people.

lead: Livagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala (KEDA), developed in Russia as one of the short peptide bioregulators associated with Vladimir Khavinson and the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology.[1][2]

Its published research is mainly laboratory work on chromatin in lymphocytes from elderly donors, along with rat studies on tissue growth and digestive enzymes. Authors report that it activates ribosomal genes and loosens condensed heterochromatin.[3][4] No controlled human trials of its effects on appearance or ageing were found. On forums it is occasionally described as a way to keep gene expression youthful, a claim not tested in published studies of skin, hair or bone.
infobox: St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, Russia

paras: Livagen is one of several short peptides, with Epitalon, Vilon, Cortagen and others, that the Khavinson group describes as tissue-specific. In organotypic culture of rat tissue, Livagen was reported to stimulate growth of liver explants, while the others stimulated brain cortex, thymus and other tissue.[2]
Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, lists the molecular formula C18H31N5O9 and a molar mass of about 461.5 g/mol, and notes that it is supplied for research as a lyophilized powder.[1]

The peptide emerged from Russian programs that began in the 1970s with animal-organ polypeptide extracts and moved to defined synthetic peptides in the late 1990s and early 2000s, according to Grokipedia.[1] Early papers on Livagen date to 2001-2002, including studies in tissue culture and in lymphocytes from older people.[3][2]

A 2002 report found that Livagen activated ribosomal genes, decondensed pericentromeric heterochromatin and released genes repressed by age-related condensation in lymphocytes from older individuals.[3] A 2007 paper in cultured lymphocytes from people aged 80 to 91 and young controls looked at Livagen combined with cobalt chloride and at heterochromatin condensation.[5] A 2004 study compared several peptides including Livagen on chromatin in subjects aged 75 to 88.[4] A 2005 rat study examined digestive enzyme activity,[6] and a 2020 paper examined the polypeptide liver complex and KEDA in normal and age-related pathology.[7] These were published mostly in Russian and Georgian journals and are in cell cultures or animals.
No studies found. The human work found uses blood lymphocytes grown in culture rather than treating people.[3][5][4]

lore.intro: A looksmax.org mini-guide presents Livagen as a bioregulator that influences DNA activity to make cells act younger.[8]
